morning.now: You ask a slab of glass a question out loud. It answers, correctly, in a pleasant voice.
morning.does: A head of brass, owned by a scholar, that answers any question put to it.

morning.now: You touch the wall and the room is as bright as noon.
morning.does: Māui and his brothers noose the sun and beat it until it agrees to cross the sky slowly, so people have light to work by.

morning.now: Breakfast is already in the house: coffee from Ethiopia, an orange from Spain, bread you did not bake.
morning.does: The self-setting tablecloth. Say "unroll" and it lays out a full meal. Say "roll up" and it clears itself.

morning.now: One machine washes last night's dishes. Another crawls round the floor eating dust.
morning.does: A lazy man says a phrase and the buckets walk home by themselves, the sledge drives without a horse and the stove carries him to the king.

morning.now: Your sister's face appears in the glass. She is across an ocean and it is evening there.
morning.tale: The silver saucer and the ripe apple
morning.does: Roll the apple round the saucer and it shows cities, fields, ships at sea and armies far away.

morning.now: She hears you laugh while you are still laughing.
morning.does: A heavenly officer who hears any sound the wind carries, however far away. His partner is the Thousand-Mile Eye.
morning.who: Chinese, Journey to the West, c. 1592

morning.now: Her voice reached you through a cable lying on the floor of the Atlantic.
morning.does: A fisherman rubs on an ointment, breathes under water and tours the cities of the sea floor with his namesake.
morning.who: Arabic, Egyptian text of the Nights, printed 1835

morning.now: You swallow a small white tablet. The kind of infection that killed the richest banker in Europe in 1836 will be gone by Friday.
morning.does: A herb that restores life. Unable to pick it out on the mountainside, Hanuman carries the whole mountain back.

morning.now: You sit in a chair eleven kilometres above the sea and are mildly annoyed by the choice of films.
morning.does: A mechanical horse that climbs when you turn the pin on its right shoulder and comes down when you turn the left.

morning.now: A bright dot crosses the evening sky. Ten people live up there. Twelve have walked on the Moon.
morning.does: She drinks the elixir, rises past the heavens and makes the Moon her home. China's Moon landers carry her name.

fly.t: 4.98 billion air passengers in a year

food.t: Haber-Bosch fertiliser, which now feeds about half of humanity
7.8% of the world undernourished, down from about a third of the developing world in 1970

speed.t: Nellie Bly round the world in 72 days
the Atlantic in about seven hours

moon.t: Artemis II carries four people round the Moon

sea.t: Trieste on the ocean floor, 10,916 m down

matches.title: A table that lays itself
matches.granted: Synthetic fertiliser (1913), refrigerated shipping (1882) and the supermarket. In the United States food now takes 6.8% of household spending.

matches.title: A thing that shows you what is far away
matches.granted: The telescope (1608), television (1926), the video call. About 6 billion people now carry one.

matches.title: Something to ride through the air
matches.granted: The balloon (1783), the aeroplane (1903), and 4.98 billion passengers in 2025.

matches.title: Water, fruit or herb that undoes death
matches.granted: Partly. Vaccines, antibiotics and surgery took world life expectancy from 32 years in 1900 to 73 in 2023. Death itself is still on the open ledger.

items.n: The Water of Life of Kāne

matches.title: Workers that are made, not born
matches.granted: The Jacquard loom (1804), the factory robot (1961), and since 2022 a machine that answers when spoken to.

matches.title: Tools that turn on their owners
matches.granted: Not a wish. A warning, recorded on three continents, that came attached to the one above.

matches.title: A visit to the Moon
matches.granted: Apollo 11 (1969). Twelve people have walked there. Four more flew round it in April 2026.

matches.title: All knowledge in one place
matches.granted: The printing press (c. 1455), the public library (1850), Wikipedia (2001) and a search box.

scientists.name: Ismail al-Jazari
scientists.work: Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices
scientists.said: Fifty machines with building instructions. One is a boat of four mechanical musicians driven by a drum with movable pegs: change the pegs and they play a different rhythm.
scientists.came: Machines that follow a changeable programme: the Jacquard loom, 1804.

scientists.name: Roger Bacon
scientists.work: Letter on the Secret Works of Art and Nature
scientists.said: It is possible that a car shall be made that will move with inestimable speed
scientists.came: The motor car, 1886. He also describes a flying device, but worked by a hand crank.

scientists.name: Leonardo da Vinci
scientists.work: Codex Atlanticus and Paris Manuscript B
scientists.said: A pyramid of linen on a wooden frame to descend from any height, and a linen screw that, turned fast enough, would bite into the air and rise.
scientists.came: The parachute, jumped in 1783. His exact design was built and jumped in 2000. The screw would not have flown.

scientists.name: Francis Bacon
scientists.said: We have also sound-houses, where we practise and demonstrate all sounds and their generation. We have some degrees of flying in the air. We have ships and boats for going under water.
scientists.came: The research institute: the Royal Society, 1660. Then acoustics, flight and the submarine.

scientists.name: Johannes Kepler
scientists.work: Open letter to Galileo, and Somnium
scientists.said: Once there are ships or sails fit for the breezes of heaven, he told Galileo, there will be no shortage of people willing to cross the void. His Somnium narrates a journey to the Moon.

scientists.name: John Wilkins
scientists.said: a flying chariot, which may be so contrived as to carry a man within it

scientists.name: Ada Lovelace
scientists.work: Notes on the Analytical Engine, Note A
scientists.said: the engine might compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity or extent.
scientists.came: Music composed by computer: the Illiac Suite, 1957.

scientists.name: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky
scientists.work: Exploration of Outer Space by Means of Rocket Devices
scientists.said: The planet is the cradle of mind, but one cannot live in the cradle forever.
scientists.came: Liquid-fuel rockets reaching orbit: Sputnik, 1957. His 1895 tower to orbit is still unbuilt.

scientists.name: Nikola Tesla
scientists.said: We shall see and hear one another as perfectly as though we were face to face. A man will be able to carry one in his vest pocket.
scientists.came: The mobile phone, 1973, and the smartphone video call, 2007.

scientists.name: Vannevar Bush
scientists.work: As We May Think, The Atlantic
scientists.said: A desk he called the memex that holds a whole personal library and lets its owner tie any two items together into named trails that others can follow.
scientists.came: Hypertext and the World Wide Web, 1991. He had the idea right and the medium (microfilm) wrong.

scientists.name: Arthur C. Clarke
scientists.said: Three relay stations parked above the equator in a 24-hour orbit would stay fixed in the sky and cover the whole planet with radio and television.
scientists.came: Syncom 3, 1964. He assumed the stations would need a crew to change the valves.

scientists.name: Alan Turing
scientists.said: In about fifty years, he guessed, a machine would fool an average questioner in a five-minute written conversation at least three times in ten.
scientists.came: In a 2025 study a language model was judged to be the human 73% of the time. Right, and a generation late.

naysayers.role: Nobel laureate, head of the Cavendish Laboratory
naysayers.said: Anyone looking for a source of power in the transformation of atoms was talking "moonshine".
naysayers.happened: Leo Szilard read the report the next morning and conceived the chain reaction that day. The first reactor ran in 1942.

naysayers.role: Astronomer, US Navy professor of mathematics
naysayers.said: Asked whether flight might be "one of the great class of problems with which man can never cope".
naysayers.happened: The Wright brothers flew at Kitty Hawk. Newcomb accepted it in 1908.

naysayers.role: Editorial, "Flying Machines Which Do Not Fly"
naysayers.said: A flying machine might be evolved "in from one million to ten million years".
naysayers.happened: The Wright brothers flew on 17 December.

naysayers.said: Space travel is "utter bilge". He added that a Moon landing would cost as much as a major war, which was not far off.
A direct steam voyage from New York to Liverpool was "perfectly chimerical".
naysayers.happened: Brunel's Great Western steamed to New York and arrived with coal to spare.

naysayers.role: Physicist, past President of the Royal Society
naysayers.said: "I have not the smallest molecule of faith in aerial navigation other than ballooning."
Of the stars: we shall "never be able by any means to study their chemical composition".
naysayers.happened: Kirchhoff and Bunsen read sodium in the spectrum of the Sun in 1859.

naysayers.said: A rocket cannot work in a vacuum. Goddard "only seems to lack the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools".
naysayers.happened: Goddard flew a liquid-fuel rocket in 1926. The paper printed its correction on 17 July 1969, with Apollo 11 on the way to the Moon.

fantasts.d: Friends' houses linked by "magnetic telegraphs". Households issue home newspapers to acquaintances in place of letters.
fantasts.arr: The telephone (1876). The blog (c. 1999).

fantasts.w: From the Earth to the Moon
fantasts.d: Three men leave Florida in an aluminium capsule, circle the Moon, splash down in the Pacific and are picked up by the US Navy.
fantasts.arr: Apollo 8 (1968): Florida, three men, Pacific, navy. Verne's cannon would have killed them.

fantasts.w: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas
fantasts.d: A large, fast, electric submarine that stays at sea for months and works as a research vessel.
fantasts.arr: USS Nautilus under nuclear power (1955), named for his.

fantasts.d: The téléphonoscope: a flat screen at home for news round the clock, plays, lessons and face-to-face calls.
fantasts.arr: Television broadcasting (1936), then streaming and video calls.

fantasts.d: Citizens pay with a "credit card". Music is piped into homes by telephone line.
fantasts.arr: Charge cards (1950). His card works like a debit card on a state allowance.

fantasts.w: Forecast for the Chicago World's Fair
fantasts.d: By 1993, food made in laboratories. A small vial would feed a person for days.
fantasts.arr: Nothing. The meal in a pill never replaced dinner.

fantasts.d: A country run by women that collects the sun's heat for power, tills fields by electricity and travels by air-car.
fantasts.arr: Solar power, electric farming, aircraft. Drawing water from the air is still rare.

fantasts.d: People live alone in rooms, meet only by screen and instant message, and depend on one global Machine.
fantasts.arr: The internet, video calls, social media, and the lockdowns of 2020.

fantasts.d: A pulsed wave bounced off a distant object to find where it is, with a diagram. Also a picture phone.
fantasts.arr: Radar (1935). Clarke called it the first accurate description.

fantasts.d: "Atomic bombs" made from an artificial radioactive element and dropped from aircraft.
fantasts.arr: The atomic bomb (1945). The physics is wrong. Leo Szilard read the book in 1932.

fantasts.d: Factory-made artificial workers replace human labour and then revolt. His brother Josef supplied the word robot.
fantasts.arr: The word, at once. The factory robot in 1961.

fantasts.d: A city of glass walls where numbered citizens live to a timetable under constant observation.
fantasts.arr: The surveillance state. A warning, and the direct ancestor of Nineteen Eighty-Four.

fantasts.d: A severed human head kept alive and conscious by machines.
fantasts.arr: Heart-lung machines and organ transplants. A head transplant has not been done.

fantasts.d: A device that focuses energy into a thin parallel beam able to cut steel at the horizon.
fantasts.arr: The laser (1960). His mirror optics could not work.

fantasts.d: Babies grown in bottles in state hatcheries. A mood drug keeps everyone content.
fantasts.arr: IVF (1978) and mass-market antidepressants. Artificial wombs are still experimental.

fantasts.d: Whole solar systems wrapped in light-traps to capture a star's entire output.
fantasts.arr: Freeman Dyson took the idea from him in 1960. None has been found.

fantasts.d: A library of every possible book, so that all truth exists and is buried in endless nonsense.
fantasts.arr: A metaphor that the web made literal. An online version went up in 2015.

fantasts.d: Glove-and-harness controls driving remote mechanical hands, stronger or finer than your own.
fantasts.arr: Remote manipulators for nuclear work, late 1940s. Engineers named them waldoes.

fantasts.d: A screen and keyboard in every home, wired to central tanks, answering any question. One loses its filters.
fantasts.arr: The home computer, the internet and search (1990s). The chatbot with failing guardrails (2020s).

fantasts.d: Thimble radios worn in the ear all day. Wall-sized television in the parlour.
fantasts.arr: Earbuds and flat-panel wall screens. He said he was trying to prevent futures.

fantasts.d: Paper books are gone. Text is stored on crystals and read on a hand-held screen called an opton.
fantasts.arr: The e-reader (2007).

fantasts.d: An ordinary family commuting by flying car, with a robot maid and video calls.
fantasts.arr: The video call and the robot vacuum arrived. The flying car in every garage did not.

fantasts.d: "Phantomatics": machine-made realities you cannot tell from the real one. Also the craft of finding your way through oceans of information.
fantasts.arr: Virtual reality and the search engine (1990s). Not in English until 2013.

fantasts.w: Visit to the World's Fair of 2014
fantasts.d: A fifty-year forecast: calls with sight and sound, cars with robot brains, wall screens. Also Moon colonies and cities under the sea.
fantasts.arr: Video calls, self-driving trials and wall screens, on time. No Moon colony, no seabed city.

fantasts.d: A palm-sized wireless communicator that flips open.
fantasts.arr: The first handheld mobile call (1973). Its maker credits Dick Tracy, not Star Trek.

fantasts.d: Astronauts watch the news on flat, book-sized screens at the breakfast table.
fantasts.arr: The iPad (2010). Samsung later cited the film as prior art against Apple.

fantasts.d: By 2001: Pan Am shuttles to orbit, a permanent Moon base, a crewed ship to Jupiter.
fantasts.arr: None of it. Pan Am folded in 1991 and nobody has landed on the Moon since 1972.

fantasts.d: The year 2010: a united Europe, China as America's rival, Detroit in ruins, satellite television, electric cars.
fantasts.arr: The European Union, China's rise, Detroit's bankruptcy, satellite TV, electric cars.

fantasts.w: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
fantasts.d: A hand-held electronic book of all knowledge, updated over the air and written by passing contributors, so patchy and unreliable.
fantasts.arr: Wikipedia (2001) on a phone. Adams started his own user-written guide in 1999.

fantasts.d: A cable from an equatorial mountain to geostationary orbit, with lifts in place of rockets.
fantasts.arr: Not built. No material is strong enough yet.

fantasts.d: The Great All-Planetary Informatorium: one worldwide databank anyone can query, with some sections restricted.
fantasts.arr: The internet, search and Wikipedia (2001).

fantasts.d: Hackers meet in a shared network world under handles. Having your real name exposed is the worst that can happen.
fantasts.arr: Online identities, handles and doxxing (1990s).

fantasts.d: "Cyberspace": a shared visual space made of all the world's computer data.
fantasts.arr: The public Web (1991), and the word. He missed the mobile phone.

fantasts.d: The "Metaverse": a permanent three-dimensional street where people appear as avatars.
fantasts.arr: Second Life (2003) and a company renamed Meta (2021). Mass adoption has not come.

who: A farmer in a village, almost anywhere. For this year the ledger is mostly blank, which is itself a fact about 1300.
The world of Napoleon and Jefferson. Fewer than one adult in eight can read.
The telephone exists, and so does the X-ray. Two children in five still die before they turn five.
Your grandparents. Penicillin has been a medicine for nine years.
dial.caption: World figures where they exist, England or the United Kingdom where they do not (food, farming, hours). Sources: [[Our World in Data|https://ourworldindata.org/]] series built on Riley (life expectancy), Moatsos (poverty), Nordhaus (light), Huberman and Minns (hours). Pre-1950 world numbers are reconstructions. "Today" is the latest year in each series, 2023 or 2024, except light, where Nordhaus stops in 1992 and LEDs have cut the figure further.

kings.name: Nathan Mayer Rothschild
kings.text: Often described as the richest man of his day. In July 1836, at his son's wedding in Frankfurt, an abscess became infected and he died within weeks. His fortune could buy anything then for sale. The cure went on sale in the 1940s and now costs less than lunch.

kings.name: Louis XIV
kings.text: In 1686 his surgeon cut out an anal fistula with a specially made scalpel and no anaesthetic. The wound took over two months to heal. In eleven months of 1711 and 1712 he lost his son to [[smallpox|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis,_Grand_Dauphin]], then his grandson, his grandson's wife and a great-grandson to [[measles|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis,_Duke_of_Burgundy]]. Both diseases now have vaccines given to infants.

kings.name: Calvin Coolidge Jr.
kings.sub: Son of the US president, died 1924 aged 16
kings.text: On 30 June 1924 he played tennis on the White House courts in shoes without socks and raised a blister on his toe. It turned septic and he was dead in about a week. His father commanded the richest country on Earth. Fleming noticed his mould four years later.

kings.name: Queen Anne
kings.sub: Queen of Great Britain, reigned 1702 to 1714
kings.text: At least seventeen pregnancies. Five children were born alive, four died before they were two, and the last, William, died at eleven. She left no heir. Her experience of motherhood was close to the average for her century, which is the point.

resonance.alt: Niels Bohr's coat of arms with a yin-yang symbol and the motto Contraria sunt complementa
resonance.doc: In 1947 Niels Bohr was given Denmark's Order of the Elephant and needed a coat of arms. He designed one around a red and black yin-yang with the motto Contraria sunt complementa, opposites are complementary. It hangs in Frederiksborg Castle.
resonance.exa: That Taoism gave him the idea. He presented complementarity at Como in 1927, twenty years before the coat of arms. He chose the symbol afterwards because it said what he meant.

resonance.src: Tao Te Ching, chapter 2. Oldest manuscript about 300 BCE
resonance.doc: The chapter says that being and non-being, hard and easy, long and short each arise from the other. It is the passage most often printed beside Bohr.
resonance.exa: The pairing is modern. Laozi's opposites are about value and perception. Bohr's are about experimental set-ups that exclude each other. The resemblance is in the shape of the thought.

resonance.alt: The diagram of the sixty-four hexagrams sent to Leibniz by Joachim Bouvet
resonance.src: I Ching, Zhou dynasty. Ordering by Shao Yong, 11th century
resonance.doc: On 1 April 1703 Leibniz received a letter from the Jesuit Joachim Bouvet in Beijing with a woodcut of the 64 hexagrams. Read broken lines as 0 and whole lines as 1 and Shao Yong's arrangement counts from 0 to 63. Within a week Leibniz posted his paper on binary arithmetic, citing the figures.
resonance.exa: That the I Ching taught Leibniz binary. He had worked it out in 1679, twenty-four years before he saw the diagram, and Shao Yong never used the arrangement to calculate.

resonance.modern: Nothing in physics. Schrödinger's own philosophy
resonance.doc: Schrödinger read the Upanishads through Schopenhauer and returned to them all his life. The closing pages of What Is Life? (1944) discuss the identity of the self with the world-soul.
resonance.exa: That Vedanta produced the wave equation, or that quantum mechanics confirms it. He kept his physics and his metaphysics in separate books and said some Eastern ideas do not fit empirical science.

resonance.src: Democritus in Greece, 5th century BCE. Kanada in India, date uncertain
resonance.doc: Two traditions, probably independent, argued that matter cannot be divided for ever and must end in smallest particles. [[Kanada|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanada_(philosopher)]] called them paramanu.
resonance.exa: That either discovered the atom. It was argument without experiment and it lost to Aristotle for two thousand years. The chemist's atom also turned out to be divisible.

resonance.src: Hindu cosmology: the Puranas and the Mahabharata
resonance.modern: The age of the Earth, about 4.5 billion years
resonance.doc: The texts set one day of Brahma at 4.32 billion years. Carl Sagan pointed out in Cosmos (1980) that this is the one old tradition whose time scales are of the right order, and added that it was surely an accident.
resonance.exa: That anyone measured anything. The figure comes from multiplying round cycle lengths, and the same texts place us 1.97 billion years into the current day, which matches nothing.

resonance.doc: Zhuang Zhou dreams he is a butterfly and wakes unable to say which of them is the dreamer. The simulation literature lists it as a forerunner, with Plato's cave and Descartes's demon.
resonance.exa: That it is the same idea. Zhuangzi is writing about how shaky our distinctions are. Bostrom's paper is a probability argument about computers.

resonance.modern: The modern source of most of these claims
resonance.doc: A bestseller in 23 languages arguing that particle physics and Eastern mysticism describe the same reality.
resonance.exa: Physicists were harsh. Jeremy Bernstein called it superficial and misleading, a confusion of similar words with similar things. The particle model it leaned on was obsolete before the book was printed.

warnings.warning: Daedalus gave two instructions: not too high, where the sun melts the wax, and not too low, where the sea soaks the feathers. Only the first is remembered.
warnings.echo: Otto Lilienthal died in 1896 after 2,000 glides. Flying now produces about [[2.5% of global CO2|https://ourworldindata.org/global-aviation-emissions]], and only about one person in ten flies in a given year.

warnings.src: Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite, c. 600 BCE
warnings.warning: A goddess wins her lover eternal life and forgets to ask for youth. He ages without end.
warnings.echo: Life has lengthened faster than health. The World Health Organization puts life expectancy at 73.3 years and healthy life expectancy at 62.8. The gap is ten years.

warnings.warning: A servant can be started by someone who does not know how to stop it.
warnings.echo: Norbert Wiener retold it in [[Science in 1960|https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/2rWfmahhqASnFcYLr/norbert-wiener-s-paper-some-moral-and-technical-consequences]], writing about automation: be sure the purpose put into the machine is the purpose you really want.

warnings.warning: A wish granted to the letter. Everything he touches turns to gold, including his dinner.
warnings.echo: The textbook picture of a machine that pursues a literal goal past what was meant. Stuart Russell builds [[Human Compatible|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Compatible]] (2019) on the problem.

warnings.warning: A made servant grows dangerous when its maker forgets to switch it off. Erasing one letter turns emet, truth, into met, dead.
warnings.echo: The line runs through Frankenstein (1818) and R.U.R. (1920) to Wiener's [[God and Golem, Inc.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_%26_Golem,_Inc.]] (1964), on machines that learn.

warnings.warning: The wooden people, made without hearts, are destroyed. Their dogs, cooking pots and grinding stones speak, and each names how it was treated.
warnings.echo: The oldest version I found of the fear that things we use carelessly will one day answer back. The Quechua recorded [[the same day|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huarochir%C3%AD_Manuscript]].

warnings.warning: What is let out cannot be put back. It was a jar. The box is a mistranslation by Erasmus.
warnings.echo: The knowledge of how to build a nuclear weapon cannot be unlearned. SIPRI counted [[12,187 warheads|https://www.sipri.org/media/press-release/2026/increasing-focus-nuclear-weapons-amid-heightened-escalation-risks-new-sipri-yearbook-out-now]] in January 2026.

warnings.warning: A god offers the king writing as a cure for forgetting. The king replies that it will breed forgetfulness and the look of wisdom without the substance.
warnings.echo: The same charge met print, calculators and [[search engines|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_effect]]. We know about the objection because Plato wrote it down.

open.step: [[Machine translation|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Translate]] went neural in 2016 and covers 249 languages, with speech and camera.
open.caveat: Nearly closed. Weak for small languages, poetry, jokes and law. Most of the world's 7,000 languages are not covered.

open.step: China certified [[EHang's pilotless two-seater|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EHang]] in 2023 and approved paid flights in 2025.
open.caveat: Short sightseeing loops from fixed pads. Not a car in every garage, and no equivalent certificate in the United States yet.

open.wish: To send a thought without speaking
open.old: Seers and mind-readers in every tradition
open.step: Brain implants decoded [[attempted speech at 62 and 78 words a minute|https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37612505/]] in paralysed patients. [[Neuralink|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuralink]] had 21 trial participants by January 2026.
open.caveat: Brain to machine, not mind to mind. It decodes intended speech and movement, not private thought. All of it is clinical trials for paralysis.

open.step: Twelve people walked there between 1969 and 1972. [[Artemis II|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program]] flew four people round the Moon in April 2026. The next landing is planned for 2028.
open.caveat: Nobody has stayed longer than about three days. No human has gone to Mars.

open.step: [[Cloud seeding|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_seeding]] has been sold commercially for decades.
open.caveat: Independent reviews find little or no effect. A Wyoming study found about 3% more snow at best. Nobody can call up a storm or stop one.

open.old: Living water, [[Gilgamesh's plant|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh]], the peaches, the elixir
open.step: A drug extends the life of mice by about a tenth. The first human trial of [[cell reprogramming|https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/01/27/1131796/]] was cleared in January 2026.
open.caveat: No treatment has been shown to lengthen human life. That first trial tests safety in the eye, not ageing.

open.step: Project CETI analysed about 9,000 sperm whale calls and found [[a combinatorial system|https://news.mit.edu/2024/csail-ceti-explores-sperm-whale-alphabet-0507]] of rhythm, tempo and ornament.
open.caveat: Structure has been found. Meaning has not. Nobody has translated a single whale sentence.

open.old: Shapka-nevidimka, the helm of Hades, the [[Ring of Gyges|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ring_of_Gyges]]
open.step: A [[metamaterial cloak|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamaterial_cloaking]] hid a copper cylinder from microwaves.
open.caveat: It was 12.5 cm wide and worked in one narrow band. Hiding a person in visible light runs into basic limits.

open.step: On 5 December 2022 a [[fusion shot|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Ignition_Facility]] gave out more energy than the laser put in: 3.15 megajoules from 2.05.
open.caveat: The laser drew about 300 megajoules from the grid to do it. No fusion plant feeds a grid, and [[ITER|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITER]] now aims at 2039 for fuel.

open.step: Colossal presented three gene-edited grey wolves as [[dire wolves|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colossal_Biosciences]].
open.caveat: Fourteen genes were edited. The specialists say these are neither dire wolves nor stand-ins for them.

open.step: Atomic clocks flown round the world [[came back out of step|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hafele%E2%80%93Keating_experiment]] with those left at home, as relativity predicts.
open.caveat: Forward only, and tiny. Six months in orbit saves about five thousandths of a second. Travel into the past has no experimental support at all.

open.step: The [[space elevator|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator]]: Tsiolkovsky's tower (1895), Artsutanov's cable (1960), Clarke's novel (1979).
open.caveat: Needs a cable far stronger than anything made. No flawless nanotube strand longer than about a metre exists.

open.step: [[Voyager 1|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_1]] left the Sun's bubble in 2012. On 18 November 2026 it reached one light-day from Earth.
open.caveat: Forty-nine years bought one light-day. The nearest star is 4.2 light-years away, more than 70,000 years at that speed.

open.old: The Sampo, the horn of plenty, the Star Trek replicator
open.step: The [[3D printer|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_printing]] shapes a material you give it. Chemists have built molecular machines that assemble a short chain step by step.
open.caveat: A general [[atom-by-atom assembler|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_assembler]] has never been built, and some chemists argue it cannot be.

open.wish: A mind that outlives its body
open.step: The complete [[wiring diagram of a fruit fly's brain|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drosophila_connectome]], about 140,000 neurons.
open.caveat: A map is not a mind. A human brain has roughly a million times more neurons.

open.wish: To be somewhere else at once
open.step: [[Quantum teleportation|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_teleportation]] moves the state of a particle, over as much as 1,400 km.
open.caveat: Only a state moves, never matter, and a normal signal is still needed to finish the job. There is no known route to sending objects.

open.step: About 600 people have been [[frozen after death|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryonics]] in the hope of revival.
open.caveat: No mammal has ever been revived from that state. The cryobiologists' own society calls it hope, not science.

open.wish: To hear from someone out there
open.old: Visitors from the sky in every mythology
open.step: Sixty-six years of [[listening|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Search_for_extraterrestrial_intelligence]] and no confirmed signal.
open.caveat: What has changed is the list of places to look: [[6,473 confirmed planets|https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/]] round other stars, against none before the 1990s.
